newsitem.title: USA: OLYMPICS-RESISTANCE SEEN TO EARLY U.S. RETURN OF GAMES.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-RESISTANCE SEEN TO EARLY U.S. RETURN OF GAMES.

text.p: American cities hoping to host the 2008 Olympic games were told Wednesday to expect international resistance to an early return of the Games to the United States.

U.S. Olympic Committee (USOC) officials, at a seminar for cities thinking of entering the lucrative Olympics-host sweepstakes, said any U.S. entry for 2008 would face negative international perceptions of last year's Atlanta Games and a feeling that other regions deserve a chance.

"What we're trying to do here is just make the cities know that 2008 is going to be a real challenge," USOC executive director Richard Schultz told reporters. "We don't want to dampen their enthusiasm."
The committee is expected to decide by May whether to back a bid for 2008, or wait until at least 2012.

Although some 40 organisations representing cities interested in USOC events attended the seminar, about eight cities -- Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Cincinnati, Houston, New York, Seattle and Washington, D.C. -- were considered to be seriously contemplating an Olympics bid, USOC public affairs director Mike Moran said.
Alfredo La Mont, director for international relations of the USOC, said: "The International (Olympic) Committee's perception of the Atlanta games is negative."
This was mostly due, Schultz said, to transport problems that marred the initial days of the Games and the heavy presence of street vendors that drew complaints of over-commercialism.
La Mont also said there is a general feeling that before the Olympics come back to North America "they should go to Europe first (in 2004) then to Africa or South America."
China, which narrowly lost out to Sydney, Australia for the right to stage the 2000 Games, would also be a serious contender, he said.
The IOC will choose a host for the 2004 Summer Games in September. After that, campaigning for the 2008 Olympics gets underway in earnest, La Mont said.
He said Paris, London, and Cairo already were preparing bids -- giving them a significant time advantage. And bids could be expected from some of the losers in the chase for the 2004 games.

A city can expect to spend $5 million to $10 million preparing a bid for the U.S. committee, and another $20 million to $30 million to prepare the bid for the international committee, Moran said. Then comes the cost of hosting the games -- in Atlanta's case, about $1.8 billion.
"It's pretty daunting," said Seattle tourism director Donna James, head of that city's bidding effort. But asked if the city was going ahead with its effort, she said, "absolutely."
